history.recordedSubject: Add the new architecture plan

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-11.*

The library started at **2.5–3.5 MB/s**, and profiling found the cost was not where it looked:

| assumption | reality |
| --- | --- |
| Key paths are the bottleneck | At ~800 cycles/byte, dispatch is single digit percent. |
| Branch misprediction matters | A naive byte-at-a-time switch already runs at 1520 MB/s, 5× the target. |
| Per-byte function calls are expensive | 0.28 ns/byte. The mode switch is another 0.35. |
| Copying a `Partial` per byte is expensive | CoW makes it O(top-level refcounted fields); ~1% difference. |

What actually cost: one malloc per byte of string content (the buffer was at refcount two at the
moment of the append), unspecialized generic `Sequence` iteration in `parse(bytes:)` (~2 mallocs
per byte cross module), and read-modify-write of whole subtrees through the computed
`\.currentElement` key path.

---

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-11.*

`StreamParseSink` receives events carrying borrowed `Span<UInt8>` and is format agnostic. Sink
methods do not throw (a sink records a failure and the parser reads it once per chunk; measured
2–5%); schema apply closures return a bool to separate an unknown key from a type mismatch, which
measured within noise. Each token has one form (`stringBegin`/`stringChunk`/`stringEnd`, keys
always whole), and escapes are decoded to UTF-8 in the parser so no `Unicode.Scalar` or `String`
reaches the sink.

history.recordedSubject: Add the new architecture plan

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-11.*

The parser finds the next byte needing attention and hands everything before it over in one
piece. Scan strategy, MB/s over an 8 KB corpus:

| run length | 4 | 16 | 64 | 4096 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| scalar | 1401 | 1480 | 1528 | 1548 |
| SWAR | 940 | 2373 | 5730 | 9817 |
| **SIMD16** | **2476** | **7469** | **12770** | **21411** |
| SIMD32 | 1680 | 2987 | 9201 | 18480 |

SIMD16 wins at every run length; SWAR is unused, and SIMD32 lowers to two operations plus a
recombine on 128-bit NEON. simdjson style structural bitmaps measured slower (byte + table 3788
MB/s, SWAR bitmap 1611, SIMD16 bitmap 2824) because structurals are 20–25% of token dense JSON.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-16.*

Whitespace outside strings varies by document:

| document | whitespace | runs | 1 byte | ≥ 16 bytes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| canada | 0% | 0 | – | – |
| llm_message | 17% | 0 | – | – |
| github_events | 19% | 2526 | 45% | 0% |
| gsoc-2018 | 19% | 41713 | 45% | 0% |
| twitter | 26% | 28826 | 46% | 2% |
| citm_catalog | 71% | 76337 | 34% | 59% |

The shipped form is one inline `<= 0x20` compare, with the SIMD16 scan out of line. The variants
below (p50 MB/s against the control) show the inlined body costing escape-heavy rows 18–35% on code
that never runs there:

| variant | citm | twitter | twitterescaped | unicode escapes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| vector body inlined | +22% | +7% | −18% | −35% |
| one byte run peeled inline | +20% | +8% | −18% | −34% |
| **shipped: one compare, then out of line** | **+21%** | **+7%** | **−1%** | **−2%** |

The one-byte peel was dropped for re-triggering that cliff. A width test keeps byte-fed input off
the vector body (it cost byte-fed `twitter` 20%), and a scalar loop behind the same early-out lost
2–5% everywhere.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-17.*

`parse` is a thin dispatcher that calls out to a function per token class, so each structural
byte cost a call, return and re-entry. `consumeStructuralRun` keeps looping while the state stays
structural, with the structural `State` cases ordered first. The `@inline` attributes are load
bearing: unforced, the optimizer inlined the run loop into `parse` and still called
`consumeStructural` per byte (function sizes in bytes):

| | HEAD | unforced | forced |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `parse` | 1284 | 1424 | **1252** |
| `consumeStructural` | 1044 | 1064 | **0** |
| `consumeStructuralRun` | – | 0 | **1240** |

Measured against controls on either side:

| document | before | after | Δ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| citm_catalog | 1211 | 1425 | +16 to +20% |
| canada | 679 | 776 | +14 to +15% |
| twitter | 808 | 911 | +10 to +16% |
| github_events | 962 | 1073 | +11 to +13% |
| gsoc-2018 | 2134 | 2187 | +2 to +4% |
| twitterescaped | 473 | 501 | +3 to +10% |
| llm_message | 1640 | 1646 | ±1% |

Corpus aggregate 1071 → 1181 MB/s (+10.2%). Byte-fed pretty printed users and unicode escaped
string lose 7–8%, but real-corpus byte-fed rows gain, so it was kept.

history.recordedSubject: SIMD Hex Quad

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-17.*

When a whole escape is in the chunk, `consumeStringRun` decodes it and keeps scanning;
`streamHexQuad` decodes the four hex digits as one `SIMD4<UInt8>`.

| document | before | after | Δ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| twitterescaped | 513 | 724 | **+41.1%** |
| twitterescaped, unchecked | 547 | 805 | **+47.2%** |
| unicode escapes (synthetic) | 410 | 1019 | **+148.5%** |
| gsoc-2018 | 2413 | 2521 | +4.5% |
| llm_message | 1712 | 1735 | +1.3% |
| citm_catalog / twitter / canada / github_events | — | — | ±0.4% |

Corpus aggregate 1259 → 1324 MB/s (+5.1%). Only simple escapes are inline: with the `\u` decode
also inline, `Fast Escaped string` lost 18.5%, and moving `fusedUnicodeEscapeEnd` out of line made
that +2.6%. Escapes with diagnostics (bad hex, lone surrogate, past the chunk) fall back to the per
byte states, keeping error offsets and resumption identical; `JSONChunkBoundaryTests` pins them at
every split.
sections.summary: When a whole escape is in the chunk, consumeStringRun decodes it and keeps scanning; streamHexQuad decodes the four hex digits as one SIMD4<UInt8>.

history.recordedSubject: SIMD whitespace scan.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-16.*

Handling whitespace in each state's unrecognised-byte arm, so minified input pays no compare, was
built and measured 10–18% slower nearly everywhere:

| document | lookahead scan | discovered in dispatch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| citm_catalog | 1214 | 1015 (−17%) |
| twitter | 818 | 681 (−17%) |
| twitterescaped | 476 | 395 (−17%) |
| github_events | 962 | 848 (−12%) |
| gsoc-2018 | 2120 | 1898 (−10%) |
| canada | 676 | 660 (−2%) |
| llm_message | 1594 | 1633 (+2%) |
| unicode escapes | 393 | 269 (−32%) |

It replaced one compare in the loop with five (one per state) plus an enum return, and even
`canada`, with zero whitespace, lost 2%; the loop is register bound, not work bound. Kept from the
attempt: `JSONConformanceTests` pins whitespace in every legal position, rejection of non-whitespace
control bytes, and rejection of a whitespace-only document.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-11.*

Superseded by "Numbers, whole": the shipped parser is a greedy SIMD16 scan with a whole-token
parse. Under per digit emission, fusing scan and accumulation measured as below (ns per number):

| variant | small | medium | large | decimals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| span only, consumer re-scans | 4.68 | 9.43 | 16.73 | 6.87 |
| fused, checked overflow | 5.27 | 13.50 | 23.20 | 8.27 |
| **fused, wrapping + digit count** | **2.96** | **7.47** | **11.91** | **5.52** |
| fused, wrapping, packed word | 3.64 | 7.27 | 11.81 | 5.60 |

The win came from dropping per-digit overflow checks, not from fusion (+17% end to end on a number
dense payload). `NumberInfo` carries magnitude, decimal exponent, digit count and flags. Per digit
reporting was later reversed: a number is now reported once, whole, `.incomplete` is gone, and
`PartialSink.number` is a plain scalar apply.

*Recorded 2026-08-11.*

Frames hold pointers into the value being built; only the innermost open container is mutated, so
buffers cannot move under an open frame. `StreamDictionary` keeps values in an append-only,
insertion-ordered array for the same reason. A frame needs a stored property, which rules out
nesting into bridged Foundation structs such as `PersonNameComponents`.

history.recordedSubject: StreamArray

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-14.*

`StreamSchema` went from a ~136 byte struct of eight closures, copied on every frame access, to a
`final class`. p50:

| | value | reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Array of structs, bulk | 251 µs | **79 µs** |
| Array of structs, view read per 4 KB chunk | 255 µs | **79 µs** |
| Array of structs, byte fed | 514 µs | **350 µs** |
| Flat struct | 9.4 µs | **6.3 µs** |
| Twitter 631 KB | 27 ms | **23 ms** |
| retains, 100 users | 13,000 | **2,101** |

Malloc counts are identical, so the cost was retain traffic from copying. Holding the schema by
pointer would save the remaining ~2,100 retains (~10%) at the cost of macro changes and an
unchecked lifetime invariant, so it was not done. A shared refcount may contend under concurrent
parses; unmeasured.

The `[String: Int]` index copies and rehashes under retention. A byte keyed flat index beats it at
every size and on every axis. ns per lookup, diverse keys:

| strategy | hit 8 | hit 32 | hit 128 | hit 512 | miss 512 | build 512 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| materialising scan (today's) | 26.0 | 59.9 | 179.7 | 664 | 1328 | 670 |
| span scan | 15.6 | 27.3 | 85.9 | 320 | 621 | 322 |
| leading word scan | 10.5 | 11.7 | 34.5 | 111 | 199 | 121 |
| whole key hash scan | 15.6 | 16.9 | 47.9 | 143 | 254 | 125 |
| `[String: Int]` | 41.6 | 33.8 | 34.8 | 35.2 | 46.9 | 119 |
| **flat chained index prototype** | **15.6** | **13.0** | **12.4** | **14.2** | **10.1** | **39.1** |

Keys sharing their first eight bytes defeat the leading word prefilter but not a whole key hash:

| strategy | hit 8 | hit 32 | hit 128 | hit 512 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| span scan | 20.8 | 43.0 | 132.8 | 549 |
| leading word scan | 26.0 | 46.9 | 148.4 | 639 |
| whole key hash scan | 15.6 | 18.2 | 47.9 | 143 |
| `[String: Int]` | 41.6 | 37.8 | 37.5 | 37.1 |
| **flat chained index prototype** | **15.6** | **15.6** | **17.3** | **17.3** |

A scan matches `[String: Int]` at ~32–128 keys, but dropping the index would cost ~9% at 128 keys
and ~43% at 512. `StreamDictionary (String lookup)` now benchmarks the shipped table directly.
Parse level retention, `BenchmarkCounts` byte fed:

| keys | discarding | window 16 | snapshot per byte |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | 9.3 µs, 13 mallocs | 19.0 µs, 21 | 17.0 µs, 21 |
| 32 | 35.0 µs, 19 | 82.0 µs, 92 | 73.0 µs, 92 |
| 128 | 141 µs, 25 | 391 µs, 380 | 356 µs, 380 |
| 512 | 601 µs, 31 | 2.37 ms, 1532 | 2.30 ms, 1532 |

Three mallocs per key under retention, and a time ratio rising from 2.0x to 3.9x, is the quadratic
term; the discarding path is flat.

Six leaking sites were found, not one:

| destination | input | was | is |

materialised slot. Wrong contents in a right shape throw `.typeMismatch`, `null` is accepted where
the destination is optional, and a container at a scalar destination stays silent (an open

history.recordedSubject: SIMD8 Digit Accumulation

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-16.*

The digit-run-to-integer step measured across block widths, ns per digit run, p50, relative to
SWAR8:

| strategy | 4d | 1–4d | 8d | 5–8d | 9–15d | 16d | 17–19d |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| scalar | 0.88x | 0.88x | 1.36x | 0.96x | 1.68x | 2.04x | 2.49x |
| SWAR4 | **0.71x** | 0.98x | 1.00x | **0.85x** | 1.01x | 1.15x | 1.26x |
| SIMD4 | 0.76x | 0.98x | 1.14x | 0.90x | 1.10x | 1.27x | 1.23x |
| SWAR8 | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x |
| **SIMD8** | 1.00x | 1.00x | **0.93x** | 0.97x | 1.03x | **0.88x** | **0.87x** |
| SIMD16 | 1.01x | 0.98x | 1.50x | 1.11x | 1.72x | 0.82x | 0.79x |
| SWAR8+SWAR4 | 0.78x | 1.02x | 1.00x | 0.84x | 0.99x | 0.95x | 1.02x |
| SIMD16+SIMD8+SIMD4 | 0.90x | 1.12x | 1.00x | 0.95x | 1.10x | 0.92x | 0.96x |

SIMD8 wins 7–13% wherever the block fires with no penalty elsewhere, so it replaced SWAR8 in
`streamParseEightDigits` (it needed the first reduction kept in `SIMD8<UInt8>` and the all-lanes
test as a 64-bit compare to avoid out-of-line calls). Narrower tiers and ladders do not pay. Digit
accumulation is ~2.2% of a `twitter.json` parse, so the change is below run-to-run variance. The
benchmark cannot be re-run because the scanners are `package`.

`consumeNumber` now does a greedy, stateless boundary scan over the number byte class, then one
structured walk (sign, integer, fraction, exponent) at the token end; a token reaching the chunk
end is buffered whole. The walk rejects `1e--2` and `1e+-2`, which the per byte rules accepted.
Malformed tokens like `1.2.3` are now one `.invalidNumber` at the token end, and an open number
contributes nothing to emitted state until it ends.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-20.*

Fusing `":` and the value's first byte into the key's closing quote gave bulk gains (`Fast
Dictionary` −16 to −20%, GitHub −7 to −12%), but every one of seven variants had a disqualifying
cost:

| variant | shape | disqualifying cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| recurse | run tail-calls itself for the fused token | the self-call is a real `bl`, not TCO'd — unbounded stack, one frame per token in a chunk; ~34K frames / 5 MB on a single-chunk GSoC, survives the 8 MB main thread and overflows a worker |
| loop, `let isKey` local | switch on the fusion, flip a local, `continue` | local spilled into the content loop; byte fed `Long string` +32%, `LLM message` +31% |
| loop, `isKeyToken` field | as above, flag read from the field | no escaped-string cliff, but the loop back-edge keeps the content loop's live ranges up: byte fed `Long string` +15%, `LLM message` +15%, `Pretty printed` +8% |
| return to dispatcher (three forms: enum, `let isKey`, field flag) | fuse, return the cursor, let `parse` re-enter — the exact shape of the accepted comma fusion | `Fast Escaped string` bulk **+62%**, in every form |
| out of line fusion helpers | the two fusions `@inline(never)` | escaped cliff gone, but the per-boundary call outweighs the structural-run it skips: `Twitter` +6%, `CITM`/`Canada`/`GSoC`/`GitHub` +3-4% |

`consumeStringRun` is at its register ceiling, so a second inlined fusion costs `Fast Escaped string`
62% even when it never runs. Rejected.

history.recordedSubject: Long decimal path

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-08-24.*

`NumberKernelBenchmarks.swift` tests two kernels over the real number extents of four corpora:
interleaving consecutive numbers, and a single vector classification that merges validation
with parsing. Every number fits a "simple decimal" shape, but lengths differ (Canada p50 18,
Twitter 3). The table is MB/s of number bytes.

| corpus | current port | single pass (32 B classify) | paired | hybrid (≤8 port, ≤16 one vector, else 32 B) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Canada (p50 18) | 1,559 | **1,887 (+21%)** | 1,962 (+26%) | **1,927 (+24%)** |
| Mesh (p50 4) | 1,226 | 1,109 (−9%) | 1,090 | 1,236 (+1%) |
| CITM (p50 9) | 1,855 | 1,290 (−30%) | 1,263 | 1,349 (−27%) |
| Twitter (p50 3) | 957 | 651 (−32%) | 707 | 853 (−11%) |

Interleaving gains only +4% on Canada: the out-of-order core already overlaps consecutive
numbers. The single-pass kernel wins 21–24% on long numbers and loses 27–32% on short ones,
because its ~10-cycle serial classification latency only amortizes past 16 digits. It is worth
taking only above 16 bytes and at least 32 bytes from the chunk end (~+10% on Canada's row).
Not built yet at this point.

| Shape | Effect on the ceiling |
| --- | --- |
| Long ASCII strings | SIMD scanning dominates; the current scanner reaches about 13 GB/s, so this shape is not representative of mixed-parser throughput. |
| Token-dense objects/arrays and small integers | Structural dispatch, event records, key routing, and branch density dominate. A structural bitmap is not automatically beneficial. |

| Small chunks or one-byte feeds | Per-call state preservation and sink checks dominate. This is a latency contract, not a realistic bulk ceiling. |

`StringSizeCensus.swift` (`STREAM_PARSING_STRING_CENSUS=1`) replays the block schedule over the

| payload | values | inline | promoted | block buffers, fragment-fed → hinted | blocks-array allocs, today → reserved |

`StreamString` is 82–84% of the typed layer's allocations on GSoC and LLM; Twitter is the control

buffers. The larger costs were bookkeeping: the `blocks` array doubling (25% of GSoC's
`StreamString` mallocs, 39% of LLM's), and a fragment-fed value re-reserving only the fragment in
hand after every sealed block.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-09-21.*

Windowed mode (`JSONParserWindow.swift`, `JSONParserShapes.swift`, the C window indexer, the
long-decimal kernel and `windowThreshold`) was deleted, about 2,300 lines; it was off by default and
won only Canada and Mesh while losing 17–30% on typed string-heavy rows. `dispatchOnce` and the
block walk's re-probe hook (`blockWalkProbeThreshold`, `parseProbing`) survived, leaving `parse` and
`consumeStructuralRun` opcode-identical.

**`JSONParser`'s size is a placement lottery, not a cache-line effect -- measured, after a false
start.** Shrinking the parser from 96 to 80 bytes first read as a ~3–4% typed loss under load; a
clean sweep over seven padded sizes showed otherwise:

| row | 80 | 88 | 96 | 96 again | 104 | 112 | 128 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Dictionary 128 keys - discarding | -0.8% | -0.8% | 0 | 0.0% | 0.0% | -0.7% | +0.1% |
| GitHub events - bulk discarding | +0.2% | -0.1% | 0 | +0.2% | +0.2% | -0.7% | -2.9% |
| Twitter - bulk discarding | +0.3% | +0.2% | 0 | +0.1% | +0.4% | -1.3% | -2.2% |
| Twitter full - bulk discarding | +0.2% | -1.0% | 0 | +0.3% | +0.7% | -0.8% | -3.0% |
| Twitter full - 16KB chunks discarding | -0.4% | -1.3% | 0 | -0.2% | +0.3% | -1.3% | -3.1% |
| Canada - bulk discarding | -1.1% | +0.1% | 0 | +0.1% | +0.1% | -0.4% | -0.1% |
| Retention 100 users - window 16 | -0.3% | 0.0% | 0 | 0.0% | -0.1% | -0.3% | -4.0% |
| Twitter - bulk (raw) | -0.5% | -0.2% | 0 | -0.2% | -0.4% | -0.4% | -0.1% |
| mean of 11 rows | -0.20% | -0.22% | 0 | +0.09% | +0.25% | -0.69% | -1.77% |

80 vs 96 is −0.2%, so the padding was removed; 128 bytes is the worst point. The response is
neither monotone nor 64-periodic, which points to sink placement. A change that grows `JSONParser`
past ~104 bytes must be swept, not A/B'd once.

**The aligned box: built, measured, rejected.** `PartialsStream` as a handle over one
line-aligned allocation of parser, sink and value, with hot code opcode-identical:

| | box, 16-aligned | box, 64-aligned |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Twitter bulk / 16 KB | -1.0 / -1.1% | -0.9 / -1.2% |
| GitHub / LLM / GSoC | -0.7 / -0.7 / -0.6% | -0.7 / -0.8 / -0.5% |
| Canada / Mesh | +0.4 / +0.3% | +0.4 / +0.3% |
| Twitter escaped byte by byte | 0.0% | 0.0% |
| mean of 20 | -0.10% | -0.28% |

64- and 16-alignment are indistinguishable, and the box costs string and object rows about a point,
so it was not kept (patch at `~/.cache/sspab/s13/aligned_box.patch`).

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-09-21.*

The classifier now emits a `scalar_end` mask (whitespace, `,` and brackets), so the walk reads a
number's end with a shift, AND and bit count instead of running `streamNumberRunEnd` per token.
Error parity holds by construction: a longer extent means a malformed token, `emitNumber` fails it
with `.invalidNumber`, and the walk hands it back to the scalar loop, which reports the same error.
As shipped (gate unchanged) the mean was +0.3%, all within the floor.

With the gate forced open, mask extents vs the scan:

| row | raw | typed |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Mesh | +20.4% | +12.7% |
| Canada | +3.9% | +8.3% |
| Numbers small integers | +31.9% | -- |
| Numbers large integers | +10.6% | +3.1% |
| Numbers floats | +8.4% | +2.6% |
| Qwen 3 workspace edit | +5.0% | +0.9% |

| GSoC / LLM | -0.2 / -0.2% | -0.6 / 0.0% |

The ungated walk against the shipped gated parser still loses, so the gate stays:

| Canada | -5.1% | -8.5% |
| Mesh | -7.4% | -11.6% |

| Twitter / CITM / GitHub / GSoC | within +-1% | within +-1% |

history.recordedSubject: Replace the block walk's strike gate with a stateless signal

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-09-21.*

The walk is entered when the ladder sees whitespace followed by whitespace or a quote, and left on a
block the classifier marks `ladder_block`; both tests depend only on the bytes at the cursor. The
census of whitespace runs that fixed the rule:

| corpus | runs | one byte | two or more |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| CITM catalog | 76,337 | 33.9% | 66.1% |
| Twitter | 28,826 | 46.3% | 53.7% |
| GitHub events | 2,526 | 45.2% | 54.8% |
| GSoC 2018 | 41,713 | 45.5% | 54.5% |
| Twitter spaced | (Python `json.dumps`) | 100% | 0% |
| Mesh | 73,024 | 100% | 0% |
| Canada / LLM / Twitter escaped / Qwen | <= 18 | -- | -- |

Against the previous strike-count gate:

| row | raw | typed |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| CITM catalog | -1.4% | +2.7% |
| Twitter full | -- | +2.5% |
| Dictionary 128 keys / Retention 100 users | -- | +2.1 / +2.0% |
| LLM message | -1.2% | +1.6% |
| GitHub events | -0.6% | +1.5% |
| GSoC 2018 | -0.6% | +1.1% |
| Qwen 3 workspace edit / structured | -0.7 / -1.6% | +1.1 / +0.3% |
| Twitter / Twitter escaped / Twitter spaced | -0.3 / -0.7 / -1.0% | +0.8 / +0.6 / +0.4% |
| byte-fed rows (6) | +0.3 .. +2.7% | |
| Canada | +1.2% | -1.4% |
| Mesh | -3.9% | **-5.5%** |
| mean of 41 rows | | +0.23% |

Mesh is the one real loss (−5.5%), from the signal's cost in the whitespace slow path. The spellings
that lost:

| spelling | what happened |
| --- | --- |
| signal on any whitespace byte; walk left only on a whitespace-free block | Mesh -7.0% raw / -10.6%: it enters on `, ` and stays |
| signal as `return ~i` to an outer driver loop that calls the walk | rows that never signal -1..-3% (Canada -1.9%, Mesh -2.9%): a second exit from the ladder's loop |
| the same signal as `i = ~i; break` | 169 stack accesses against 191, and *worse*: Canada -5.2%, Mesh -6.0% |
| two whitespace bytes only (no quote) | Twitter spaced -5.0%: Python-style objects want the walk |
| signal read off the scan's results (run >= 2, or stopped on a quote) | Mesh -3.2% but Canada raw -7.1%, Qwen raw -5.5%, `Pretty printed users - 64B` -10.6%, Qwen typed -1.6% |
| lookahead byte reused: when it is neither whitespace nor a quote it goes straight to the dispatch (`i += 1; byte = next`), skipping the scan | Mesh +3.6% (raw +2.1%), and the rest down: Twitter escaped -3.5%, Retention -2.9%, Canada -2.6%, Qwen -2.6/-2.4%, Twitter full -2.1%; raw Canada -4.5%, Qwen -5.2/-5.0% (mean -1.43%, floor -0.22%). 21 fewer instructions and 19 fewer stack accesses in the `NullSink` run; the compiler gave the shortcut its own edge into the token dispatch (and a free `next >= 0x40` tier) |
| the same, as `i += 1; continue` (no new edge into the dispatch; the byte is reloaded at the loop head) | 8 rounds, Mesh floor 0.0%: Mesh **+2.8%**, Mesh 16KB +0.7%, raw Mesh -2.4%; CITM -0.5%, Canada 0.0%; Twitter spaced -2.8% and Twitter escaped -2.4% on rows whose floor read -1.6% and -1.8% in that run. Not rejected by these numbers alone; re-tried on top of the fused signal below and closed there (Mesh -3.8%, LLM -2.5%) |

The signal was then fused into one AND and one branch (`signalBitmap` as a computed `static var`,
since a `static let` cost a lazy addressor call). `sig` is the fused test; `sigfus` adds the
`i += 1; continue` shortcut:

| row | `sig` raw / typed | `sigfus` raw / typed |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GSoC 2018 | +2.8 / +1.0% (16KB +0.9%) | +2.3 / +0.3% |
| CITM catalog | +2.4 / +0.7% (16KB +1.2%) | +0.8 / +1.2% |
| GitHub events | +0.6 / +0.5% | +0.5 / +0.8% |
| Twitter / spaced / full | +0.8 / +0.8 / -- ; +0.4 / +0.2 / +0.3% | +0.9 / +1.0 / -- ; +0.7 / +0.1 / +0.8% |
| Qwen 3 structured / workspace edit | 0.0 / 0.0 ; +0.7 / 0.0% | +0.8 / +1.1 ; -0.1 / -1.0% |
| LLM message | -1.3 / 0.0% (16KB +0.2%) | +1.5 / **-2.5%** (16KB -2.2%) |
| Mesh | -2.0 / -0.9% (16KB +0.5%) | +2.2 / **-3.8%** (16KB -0.6%) |
| Twitter escaped | +0.7 / -0.3% | +0.9 / -0.9% |
| Canada (24 whitespace bytes: never signals) | -1.3 / -2.6% (16KB -2.6%) | +0.1 / -4.5% |
| Retention 100 users / Dictionary 128 keys (minified: never signal) | +3.2 / +0.8% | +3.0 / +2.3% |
| mean of 34 rows | +0.22% | +0.11% |

`sig` landed; `sigfus` is closed (LLM typed −2.5%, Mesh typed −3.8%).

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-09-22.*

A sink requirement (`stringStorage()`, `lendsStringStorage`) let `PartialSink` lend the
`StreamString` tail so staging stored straight into it, removing the flush copy. Fixing three codegen
traps on the way (bridgeable `[StreamBlock<UInt8>]`, `blocks = []` allocating, and an `init()` that
assigns fields in its body costing two retain/release pairs per value) brought it from −5.6% to the
final shape:

| Twitter spaced | | -0.9% |

| Qwen workspace / structured | | -0.6% / -0.2% |

history.recordedSubject: Condense markdown

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-09-16.*

Four findings: (1) shared-tail appends after a copy overwrote each other's slots, since resolved by
the copy-on-write change below; (2) dictionary lookup changes canonical-equivalence behaviour once a
key stops being pending; (3) malformed UTF-8 character traversal can emit content twice; (4) public

history.recordedSubject: Log the session's six landed changes and point the explorer at them
history.revisedSubject: Log the session's six landed changes and point the explorer at them

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-09.*

"Landed: ordinary copy-on-write on streaming collection tails" put a uniqueness check in
`StreamArray.nextSlot()`, and the typed number-array and fixed-width element appends paid it per
element: an outlined `ensureUniqueTail` calling `swift_isUniquelyReferenced_native` through a dyld
stub. In the baseline profiles typed Mesh spent 5.2% in `isUnique`, 3.4% in the stub and 4.6% in
`ensureUniqueTail`, and Canada about 2.9%; CITM, GitHub, GSoC, LLM and Qwen showed at most 0.6%,
so the dictionary and string paths were left alone. Three changes:

- `nextSlot` inlines the test and outlines only the copy (`copySharedTail`), so every append path
  loses the `ensureUniqueTail` frame.
- `PartialSink.knownUniqueTail` holds the address of a tail block the sink has proved unique during
  the current parse call. `arrayDouble` / `arrayInt` appends and the SIMD element opens go through
  `nextSlot(knownUniqueTail:)`, which skips the runtime call on a hit. The address is forgotten at
  `commit()` (the end of every parse call), at `reset()`, and after an `onFieldRecognized` hook
  runs, since the hook is caller code that can copy a member mid-call. Debug builds still assert
  the claim.
- `appendHomogeneousInt` is `@_transparent`. With the extra `inout`, `@inline(__always)` stopped
  holding and `number` tail-called an outlined copy with its own five-pair prologue.

The `Double` hit path is `ldr` tail, `ldr` known, `cmp`, `b.ne`, `ldr` count, `ldr` capacity,
`cmp`, `b.ge`, `add`, with no call. Nine tests in `SinkTailUniquenessTests`; removing the
`commit()` / `reset()` clears fires the debug assert in them.

sections.chapter: Landed: the arm64 UTF-8 validator keeps every byte in registers

history.recordedSubject: Log the session's six landed changes and point the explorer at them
history.revisedSubject: Log the session's six landed changes and point the explorer at them

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-09.*

`streamValidateUTF8Shimmed` built its first block, a short run and the tail in a 32-byte
zero-padded stack scratch. In the baseline binary that was a prologue saving x19–x22, a
stack-protector load and check, `stp q0, q0` and `bl memcpy` for the first block and again for the
tail, `ldur q` reloads that read 16 bytes back from byte stores (a store-forwarding failure), and
the three tables and the accumulator spilled around the tail's `memcpy`.

The run loop is now `stream_parsing_utf8_validate_neon` in the shim, and no byte goes through
memory. The first block's previous-byte views are `ext` against zero
(`stream_parsing_utf8_first_block_errors`). A run shorter than sixteen bytes is the sixteen bytes
ending at `to` with the lanes before `from` cleared, or, when fewer than sixteen bytes precede
`to`, assembled from overlapping loads inside the run (`stream_parsing_load_short_u8`). The tail
is the sixteen bytes ending at `to`, its views loads except for a 17- or 18-byte run, where they
are the first block shifted in from zero. The kernel reads `[0, to)` of `base`, which every
caller's base (the chunk, the parser's buffer, the `parse(byte:)` scalar) satisfies; a test runs
every length 0...80 at offsets 0...33 in an exactly sized allocation, and under ASan catches an
injected read past `to`. `streamValidateUTF8` became a frameless leaf.

Then `validateNonASCIIRun` inlines the kernel (`streamValidateUTF8Inline`), and the scalar walk and
the throw move to a static `@inline(never)` `failInvalidUTF8` in tail position. A valid run is one
call with a frame record, where it was two calls and six saved registers.

history.recordedSubject: Log the session's six landed changes and point the explorer at them
history.revisedSubject: Log the session's six landed changes and point the explorer at them

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-09.*

Three changes on the typed layer's member and element open path.

- **Template copies.** `_streamCopyInitialize` takes the value-witness path above 128 bytes
  (was 1024). Below the threshold `initialize(to:)` stages the value, and from 64-byte structs with
  three refcounted fields up that compiled to a `memcpy` from the template to a stack temporary, a
  `memcpy` from the template to the slot, and an outlined `initializeWithCopy` of the temporary
  into a second, dead one, which is where the retains happen; only values of 48 bytes or fewer
  stayed inline. The same shape was in the `GitHubPayload.Partial?` prepare (721 B), the
  `CITMArea.Partial` element open (60 B) and the mid-size prepares (176 B).
  `_streamCopyInitializeSome` copies an optional template's payload through the payload's own
  witness plus its trivial tag bytes, skipping `Optional`'s generic witness; the optional-member
  prepare and the dictionary value open use it.
- **Field prepares.** `StreamFieldTable.prepares` holds each closure in a `_StreamFieldPrepareBox`,
  retained once and stored as an address, and `valueTarget` calls it through
  `_withUnsafeGuaranteedRef`. Loading the closure out of `UnsafePointer<StreamFieldPrepare?>` was
  an outlined copy (a retain), a call at maximal abstraction through a reabstraction thunk with both
  arguments spilled, and an outlined consume (a release), per member open.
- **Generic containers construct.** `StreamArray` and `StreamDictionary` set
  `_streamOpensByConstruction` and make `init()` / `streamInitialValue()` `@inlinable`. Their
  template copy was the generic struct witness walking every field through metadata, on every
  optional array or dictionary member and every array-of-arrays element opened.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-09.*

`coalescedEscapedStringTail` restarts its 16-byte scan at every escape and leaves it through a
data-dependent reduction: one mispredicted branch per escape. Census of the escaped tails:

| Payload | Bytes in escaped tails | Escapes | Shape |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| LLM message | 96.4% | 14,222 simple, 0 `\u` | 546 tails, median 1,870 B; runs between escapes median 9 B, mean 68 B; 5,833 of 15,855 blocks hold an escape, 5,080 hold non-ASCII |
| GSoC 2018 | 47.7% | 13,721 simple, 1,292 `\u` | no non-ASCII; 16,108 of 23,973 blocks hold no escape |
| Twitter escaped | 36.7% | 1,228 simple, 31,818 `\u` | 10.4 escapes per block |

`stream_parsing_unescape_blocks` (`StreamParsingShims/Unescape.c`, out of line) copies string
content to the coalescing buffer 64 bytes at a time, decoding escapes and validating UTF-8 in the
same pass, with no branch on where the escapes are. Every block is stored whole, and two escapes
are decoded whether or not the block has two: an absent one is given position 64, where its stores
land past the output cursor. A third escape, a stop and `\uXXXX` (surrogate pairs included) take
one out-of-line walk of the block. UTF-8 is checked over the source with
`stream_parsing_utf8_block_errors`: one vector placed a byte ahead of the block's first non-ASCII
group, all four when the non-ASCII bytes span more than three groups, for sixteen blocks from any
block with a non-ASCII byte, and none in text without one. The result comes back in two registers
(bytes consumed; bytes produced shifted left two, with the reason in the low bits).

`JSONParser.coalescedEscapedBlocks` calls it at the top of the tail's loop, on entry and again
after the per-run loop takes a run of 64 bytes or more. The kernel hands the value back to the
per-run loop at the closing quote, at anything with a diagnostic, within 139 bytes of the chunk
end, and after sixteen blocks with no escape. The per-run loop is the fallback for all of them,
so error offsets are its own. x86_64 and the portable build keep the per-run loop alone.

Mutations of the carry, trimming, windowing, slot offset, quiet and invalid exits, the terminator
constant, the validation run and the `\u` rules were each caught by `EscapedTailBlockTests`.

`streamAccumulateDigits` gives each eight bytes before the token end one SWAR class test
(`streamDigitClass`) that serves both outcomes. All numerals is a full block, converted from the
same subtraction (`streamEightDigitValue`); otherwise the run ends inside the word, and its leading
numerals are one shift, one conversion and one multiply by 10^count
(`streamAccumulateLeadingDigits`, with `stream_parsing_pow10_u64`). With fewer than eight bytes
left, the eight ending at the token end are read and shifted down. In the integer segment one byte
left is one step (CITM's nine-digit ids). Only a buffer shorter than eight bytes keeps the byte
loop. This replaces the SIMD eight-digit block, whose class test could not be reused, and the
per-digit loop of dependent multiplies. `emitGeneralNumber` went from 34 NEON instructions to 2
(320 → 416 instructions) in the `FastCountingSink` specialisation and from 128 to 0 (1,280 →
1,664) in `PartialSink`'s.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-10.*

`twitterescaped` holds 31,818 `\u` escapes in 1,715 runs (mean run 18.5) and 1,228 simple
escapes; 31,770 of the `\u` escapes are three-byte scalars, 28 two-byte, and 10 are surrogate
pairs. The coalescing tail answered each one by decoding it, scanning a zero-length run, reading
the next backslash and calling back in.

- `coalescedUnicodeEscapeEnd` keeps decoding while the next bytes are another escape it can take
  whole (a `\uXXXX`, a surrogate pair, or a simple escape), with the buffer's fill count held in a
  register, and returns where the first escape it cannot take starts. Which escapes fall back to
  the per-byte states, and every error offset, are unchanged. The unbuffered arm (a key's escape)
  keeps `fusedUnicodeEscapeEnd`, one escape per call.
- `streamHexQuad` validates and decodes four digits with SWAR range tests in one 32-bit register
  instead of SIMD4, whose result crossed from a vector register (`uminv` + `fmov`, `addv` + `fmov`).

Profile of raw Twitter escaped with v3: the tail 17% → 3.6%, the staging scan 8.2% → 2.2%, the
escape function 29% (it absorbs `bufferStringScratch`). New tests: the hex quad against a
per-character decode on every byte in every lane, a `\u` run cut at every offset with 64- and
4096-byte buffers, a run delivered as one chunk.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-10.*

`stream_parsing_classify_skip_block` loads its block with `vld4q_u8`, so vector j lane i holds byte
4i + j, and builds each of its five masks with `stream_parsing_movemask4_deinterleaved`: three
shift-right-inserts stack the four vectors' top bits into one lane's high nibble, a fourth copies
the nibble down, and `shrn #4` packs the word. That replaces four `and`s and three `addp`s per mask.
Only bit 7 of each lane is read, so the bracket class, which is bit 7 of the class byte, needs no
test, and the accepted test lowers to one `cmtst` instead of `and` / `cmeq` / `bic`. The skip loop
advances by 64 whatever the masks say, so it runs at the kernel's throughput and the extra latency
of `ld4` is hidden.

The kernel alone, ns per 64-byte block, min of 30 repetitions (load about 100). The dependent
column chains each block's quote mask into the next address:

| Variant | Twitter | CITM | GSoC | LLM | Twitter, dependent |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| four loads, `movemask4` (base) | 8.56 | 8.03 | 6.73 | 4.97 | 16.01 |
| `ld4` + shift-insert | 7.93 | 7.05 | 6.85 | 5.22 | 17.77 |
| `ld4` + shift-insert, brackets from bit 7 (landed) | 7.61 | 6.75 | 6.74 | 5.20 | 17.60 |
| `uzp`, brackets from bit 7 | 7.87 | 6.92 | 6.94 | 5.42 | |

GSoC and LLM blocks are mostly inside strings, where the kernel returns after two masks; `ld4`
gains nothing there. Every corpus at 64 phases under zero and chained carries, 1 MB of random bytes,
and every byte value at every position classify identically. `BlockClassifierTests` holds both
classifiers, field by field, to a byte-at-a-time restatement; swapping one shift-insert's operands
fails it.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-10.*

Three changes on the typed layer's key and open paths.

- **`key`.** It saved six register pairs per key (236 instructions): the table scan called
  `streamFieldTailMatches` from inside its loop and kept nine values live across the call. The scan
  (`matchTableKey`) now stops at the first entry whose first word and length match; a key of at
  most a word is stored there, and a longer one tail-calls `matchTableKeyTail` (linear and indexed
  forms), a leaf with the tail compare inline. The dictionary and closure arms are tail-called
  helpers (`dictionaryKey`, `closureKey`). `key` is frameless, 116 instructions, and
  `@inline(never)`: at that size the walk inlined it, `consumeStructuralBlocks<PartialSink>` grew
  1383 → 1550 instructions and `consumeStructuralRun` 1919 → 1973, and typed Twitter, GitHub and
  Qwen structured lost 2.0–3.7%.
- **String element and dictionary-value opens.** `_openElement(_:)` drained the closed element,
  re-marked the box `nil`, then assigned over it, destroying that `nil` out of line through the
  optional's metadata (`getEnumTagSinglePayload` and a mangled-name lookup) per element.
  `StreamString` and `StreamString?` elements open with `_openElement(constructing:)` and the
  dictionary string routes with `_openValue(forKey:constructingSome:)`. The destroy is left only on
  an array's first open.
- **Template copies of 128 to 1024 bytes.** `_streamCopyInitialize` copies through `_streamCopyOut`,
  an unspecialised function (`@_semantics("optimize.sil.specialize.generic.never")`) that is six
  instructions: a tail call into `T`'s `initializeWithCopy` witness writing the indirect result. The
  caller moves the result into the slot with one `memcpy`. `initialize(from:count:)` reached the same
  witness through `swift_arrayInitWithCopy` and a type-descriptor lookup. Above 1024 bytes the runtime
  path stays; Embedded Swift keeps it throughout.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-10.*

Census: Canada's 111,126 numbers are 101,338 past Clinger's tier (91%), 9,742 exact and 46
integers, with 17,775 transitions between those classes; Mesh's 73,014 are 40,614
integers and 32,400 exact, none past Clinger. `number` saved twelve registers (342 instructions)
for every `[Double]` / `[Int]` element and SIMD lane because the object-table arm was inlined into
it, and each `Double` went through two more frames, the generic initializer and an outlined
Eisel–Lemire.

- **A frameless `number`.** The three homogeneous routes finish with no call when the token
  converts on the exact tier (`streamParseDoubleExact`, `streamParseIntExact`) and the slot is
  ready: `StreamArray.appendClosedIfReady` (no open element, room in a tail already proved unique)
  or a lane inside the arity. Every miss tail-calls the outlined full path
  (`appendHomogeneousDouble` / `Int`, `storeSIMDDoubleLane`), the typed slots tail-call
  `applyKnownNumber`, and the object and closure routes tail-call `numberRouted`.
  `streamEiselLemire` is forced inline, so the full paths hold the kernel in their own frame.
  `number` was then 128 instructions and saved no registers; a `[Double]` hit is about 40
  instructions ending in `ret`. A first version that outlined only the default arm kept five pairs: any call in
  the function keeps the frame. It was not measured.
- **SIMD elements open and close without a call.** `beginArray` opens a non-optional
  `SIMD2/3/4<Double>` element itself when nothing needs a call
  (`openSIMDDoubleElementIfReady`: `StreamArray.openElementIfReady`, the frame pushed inline, the
  schema from the parent's element schema so the global's lazy accessor stays off the path). The
  full open (`openKnownSIMDDoubleElement`) is tail-called and pushes through `pushSIMDDoubleFrame`,
  with the route word and cursor written as constants. `endArray` closes a lane frame with the
  arity from the route and the pop inline, framelessly; anything else tail-calls `endArrayRouted`.
- **Lanes ask Eisel–Lemire first.** In the profile of the two changes above, the hottest instruction
  in `number` (4.6% of typed Canada's samples) followed Clinger's `<= 2^53` branch: 9% of Canada's
  coordinates are exact at random positions. A lane now tail-calls `storeSIMDDoubleLaneByKernel`,
  which converts with `streamParseDoubleKernel` (`@_transparent`; as `@inline(__always)` it stayed a
  call) and stores with no frame; a decline or an arity overflow tail-calls the full lane path.
  Every tier is correctly rounded, so values are unchanged. Lanes that are short exact decimals
  (Mesh's influences) now pay the kernel instead of an `fdiv`.

In typed Canada the sink's share went from 31.1% (`number` 4.4, the initializer 7.4, Eisel–Lemire
10.5, `openKnownSIMDDoubleElement` 3.5, `endArray` 2.9, `pushFrame` 2.4) to 26.8%
(`storeSIMDDoubleLane` 12.4, `number` 8.5, `beginArray` 3.6, `endArray` 2.3) before the third
change. `HomogeneousNumberRouteTests` pins the routes' values and refusals at every chunk size; the
float differential pins `streamParseDoubleInline` to the initializer on both corpora, the edge
tokens and 20,000 seeded random decimals, and the kernel alone on every token.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-10.*

The kernel alone over every escaped tail took 166.5 µs on Twitter escaped (52.7 ns a block, 5.2 ns
a `\u`), against 169.5 on LLM message and 220 on GSoC. 85% of `twitterescaped`'s escapes are in runs
of eight or more three-byte scalars.

- `stream_parsing_unescape_bmp_run` (out of line, entered from the block walk when the bytes 6 and 18
  past the escape's backslash are backslashes too) checks the shape of four escapes with NEON and, when all four are
  three-byte non-surrogate scalars, writes their twelve UTF-8 bytes from two `tbl` gathers and two
  per-lane shifts (`stream_parsing_unescape_four_bmp`); then two more for a run's remainder. A run
  may continue past its block as far as the chunk's and the buffer's slack allow. It first turns
  away an escape whose digits, or the next one's, begin with `0` or `d`/`D`.
- A surrogate pair inside a block is decoded as two six-byte escapes, so a decode never edits the
  walk's escape mask. Taking twelve bytes made the walk clear the partner's bit with a `csel` on
  `taken`, which put the decode on the path to the next escape's position.
- The kernel keeps its own copy of the three UTF-8 tables; `EscapedTailBlockTests` holds them to the
  Swift ones through `stream_parsing_unescape_utf8_table`. Its callers, out-of-module sink
  specialisations, called three getters per entry.
- The run's branch is marked unlikely so LLVM saves the vector registers around the call rather
  than at every entry to the walk.

The kernel alone on Twitter escaped:

| Step | µs |
| --- | ---: |
| pairs as two escapes (v1) | 161.7 → 149.5 |
| four at a time, inline, constants hoisted into d8–d15 (v2) | 85 |
| the run out of line (v3) | 87.5 |
| the run past its block (v5; bounded to the block's slack, 85.2) | 70.2 |
| the two-escape remainder (v8) | 69.0–70.7 → 62.9–65.8 |

On `Fast Unicode escaped string` (two-byte scalars and surrogate pairs) the kernel alone took 4.9 µs
before this, 13.6 with the shape check unguarded and 8.8 with the lead-digit test. Twelve mutations
of the shape check, the pair rules, the run advance and the remainder were each caught by the new
tests.

sections.markdown:
*Recorded 2026-11-10.*

Raw Twitter escaped byte by byte read +8.6% to +9.1% in the walk gates (K2, v12), the skip
classifier's gate, the key and copy gate, and the `\u` loop measured on top of the kernel; Pretty
printed byte by byte +3.3% to +3.7%, typed LLM byte by byte -3.4%. Those rows never run the block
walk, and `parse`, `consumeStringRun` and `consumeStructuralRun` were opcode-identical. K2b alone puts
`parse`, `consumeStringRun`, `consumeStructuralRun` and `coalescedEscapedStringTail` at the same
addresses as the K2 pair and reads +3.2% / +0.2% where the pair reads +8.7% / -3.3%, so 128-byte
alignment of those functions does not explain it. The mechanism was not identified. Against the
session's start the row reads +0.3%.
